messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error of the sample mean (under the null)**  

The “standard deviation” of the sampling distribution of the sample mean—i.e., the standard error—is calculated as:

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
- \(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
- \(n = 40\) (sample size)

\[
SE = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.221
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test (the standard error of the mean) is **≈ 0.22**.  

*(If you were instead asking for the standard deviation of the t‑statistic itself, that would be 1 for a t‑distribution with 39 degrees of freedom.)*
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis. The standard error is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they might want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That is indeed the standard error: sigma / sqrt(n). So compute 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So about 0.221.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic? The test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the test statistic under null is 1 (for t distribution with df=39). But they ask "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" which is ambiguous. They gave sample mean, standard deviation, sample size, population mean. They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. That could be the standard error of the mean. So answer: 0.221.

We can also mention that the standard error is 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.221. So the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null is 0.221. If they want the standard deviation of the t-statistic, it's 1. But likely they want the standard error.

Thus answer: approximately 0.221. Provide explanation.
